content.p: Three men who had come to Central Florida for a car show were shot dead on the afternoon of Saturday 17 January 2026, outside the rental house where they were staying near Kissimmee. They were stuck there with rental-car trouble and getting ready to go home. The Osceola County Sheriff's Office arrested the man who lived next door, Ahmad Jihad Bojeh, who was 29. He has been indicted on three counts of first-degree murder and has not been tried. Nothing about the killings has been decided in court.

The case drew attention beyond the shootings for a second reason. In 2021 Bojeh had been charged with attempted first-degree murder after a shooting at a gas station, and in December 2022 a judge found him not guilty by reason of insanity. Florida's attorney general and the local state attorney then argued publicly over how that case had ended. In September 2026 a different question was settled: a judge ruled, after hearing from court-appointed psychiatrists, that Bojeh is competent to stand trial.
content.h2: The shooting at Indian Point Circle
content.p: According to the sheriff's office, deputies were told of a shooting at 12:14 p.m. and reached 296 Indian Point Circle, in the Indian Point subdivision, where they found three men dead in front of the house. All three had been shot. The sheriff's timeline said that multiple 911 calls reported shots fired, that deputies arrived at 12:19 p.m. and that they saw a man running toward the house next door.

The dead were Robert Kraft of Holland, Michigan, his brother Douglas Kraft of Columbus, Ohio, and their friend James Puchan. Sheriff Christopher Blackmon said the group had begun as four men. One had left the day before, and he was the twin of Douglas Kraft. The families said the men were in Kissimmee for the Mecum car show and had been waiting for help with their rental car. Ages vary between outlets: the sheriff gave Robert Kraft as 70 and Puchan as 69, while FOX 35 later reported them as 69 and 68. Douglas Kraft was 68 in every account.

Blackmon called the shootings random and "cold-blooded", and said there was no known conflict between the victims and the man who lived next door. "It just happened to be the person who lived next door," he said at a Sunday news conference. He also described the killings as premeditated. Early statements did not offer a motive.

A joint statement from the families described the three as "beloved husbands, fathers, grandfathers, uncles, brothers and friends". It said there were no known interactions between the men and Bojeh before the event.

Deputies detained Bojeh at his home. Blackmon said the quick response meant deputies questioned him inside the house and kept him away from the public, since otherwise there might have been other victims. Two firearms were recovered. On the day after the killings the sheriff said work was still going on to establish whether either had been used. FOX 35, citing an arrest affidavit, later reported that two pistols were found hidden under a bed and that the pistols matched the calibers of the rounds found at the scene. Spectrum News, citing court filings, also reported two handguns under his bed.

The same affidavit, as FOX 35 reported it, said Bojeh loudly refused to comply while deputies carried out a search warrant for blood, demanded a lawyer, tensed his body and resisted, and shouted slurs and profanities. At a first appearance on Sunday 18 January a judge found probable cause to hold him without bond. He had a public defender and said nothing. Outlets also reported that on the Monday he did not speak and would not give his name.

The sheriff's office said it had received 41 calls for service to the Bojeh family address between September 2006 and April 2022, 16 of which involved Ahmad Bojeh, most when he was a minor. Most were from his father, who told deputies his son was skipping school or acting aggressively toward relatives. Blackmon called him a "frequent flier" at the sheriff's office. FOX 35 reported that as an 18-year-old he was on probation for drug charges when he was arrested again for possession of drugs and paraphernalia. The Osceola News Gazette reported that he was also arrested in 2015 over a felony drug possession charge, and again in 2020 for resisting an officer without violence. Those charges were dropped, or adjudication was withheld.
FOX 35 also quoted letters from Bojeh's father to a judge. In one, the father wrote that his son "has been sitting home since 2014" with no income.
content.h2: The 2021 case and the insanity verdict
content.p: In May 2021 Bojeh was charged with attempted murder over a shooting in the parking lot of a Wawa on West U.S. 192 in Kissimmee. The Osceola News Gazette wrote that police said he fired a gun at parked vehicles, at least one of them occupied. FOX 35 reported that the case also carried counts of aggravated battery and two counts of criminal mischief besides attempted first-degree murder with a firearm, and described a man shot several times and a car crash.

After more than a year of competency evaluations, the case was tried by a judge alone rather than a jury. On 20 December 2022 Circuit Judge Keith Carsten found Bojeh not guilty by reason of insanity. The next day he was released on conditions: mental health treatment, taking prescribed medication, having no access to firearms and no contact with victims or witnesses. He was to receive outpatient care at Park Place Behavioral Health in Kissimmee. FOX 35 reported that the State Attorney's Office and the defence agreed to skip a jury and to outpatient treatment, and that the doctor who evaluated him for the defence found he no longer met the standard for involuntary commitment to a state hospital. Prosecutors did not retain their own expert, FOX 35 said.

Court filings quoted by Spectrum News show that a mental health specialist told the court in 2023 that Bojeh was keeping his appointments and taking his medication and had a job at McDonald's. The Osceola News Gazette reported that treatment stopped in 2023 when the cost went up. Worrell said she understood it had risen from $7 a month to more than $150 and that he fell out of compliance because he could not pay. Migdalia Perez, the lawyer who represented him in 2021, told FOX 35 that Park Place allegedly did not report to the court when he stopped taking his medication.

On 19 January, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier wrote on X that Worrell "didn't put up a fight to Bojeh's use of the insanity defense, and he was allowed to go free", and in another post that she had "knowingly stipulated to an agreement" that avoided a jury trial. He pointed to her 2023 suspension from office by Ron DeSantis, who had cited "neglect of duty and incompetence". Worrell was elected again in 2024.

Worrell replied that the case "was fully litigated at trial", that the court rather than the prosecutor determined the outcome, and that the attorney general misunderstood the facts and the law. She also said that once a court finds a person is no longer a danger to himself or others, the law bars involuntary commitment to a mental hospital. FOX 35 reported that Uthmeier was pushing to change Florida's insanity law so that anyone acquitted on that ground would be held in a secure mental health facility for the full term of the sentence, with no early release. He said in February that he would like to see the death penalty pursued.
content.h2: Charges, delays and the competency fight
content.p: Outlets differ on the first charge. ClickOrlando and CBS Miami reported that he would face first-degree murder counts after his arrest, and FOX 35 reported that he was booked on three counts of first-degree murder with a firearm. Later FOX 35 reports, though, said that Worrell's office had charged three counts of second-degree murder, and that a first-degree charge required a grand jury indictment. Uthmeier said of the lower charges on 12 February, "That's not enough."

Bojeh refused to attend his arraignment. A judge ordered him to appear in person, but at the hearing on Wednesday 18 February he again refused to be transported. His public defender asked for a competency evaluation. Prosecutor Peter Donnelly told the court that Bojeh got up to eat and use the toilet and was "treating this as a voluntary program". Prosecutors said he became catatonic when required to attend hearings or see doctors. Judge Wooten appointed a doctor and said he would order Bojeh into the courtroom only if it became necessary.

On 26 February a grand jury indicted Bojeh on three counts of first-degree murder. Worrell said her office would consider referring the case to its capital case review panel, which weighs whether the death penalty is appropriate. The Osceola News Gazette said the notice of intent to seek the death penalty normally falls due 45 days after arraignment. In April, FOX 35 reported that prosecutors asked to extend that period to 120 days, citing defence witnesses in the Middle East who were hard to reach, and the Gazette reported the court granted the extension. No decision on the death penalty had been reported by the time of the September competency ruling.

On 18 June a competency hearing was delayed when a substitute judge sat in for Wooten and the two sides could not agree on what two completed psychiatric evaluations showed. At a status hearing the next day Wooten ordered a third evaluation, by a psychiatrist, over defence objections. Prosecutors wanted the doctor to look at his jail medication and whether he was malingering, which means deliberately faking symptoms. The defence argued that evaluations connected to the 2021 case had no bearing on this one.

On 9 September FOX 35 reported that newly unsealed evaluations from at least two court-appointed psychiatrists concluded that Bojeh was exaggerating or fabricating symptoms to avoid prosecution, although he said he heard voices. Wooten refused to keep the evaluations sealed, saying there was great public interest in understanding how the competency process works. At the hearing on Thursday 10 September, a psychiatrist testified that Bojeh had deliberately done badly on testing: his score was so improbable, the doctor said, that it would occur about once in 33 billion tries by chance. The doctor said he does have psychosis, but that it can be treated with medication and does not stop him from understanding the proceedings or helping his lawyers. Wooten ruled him competent to stand trial.

Bojeh is next due in court in November. He remains charged and is presumed innocent. The charges are accusations, no plea has been reported, and the 2022 finding of insanity concerned only the earlier case.
